body:
Found while working #885.

**What happens:** `assets/posts/doosan-dnm.cps` on a 4th axis without TCP (`machine.rtcp` false - e.g. an A that states no tilting direction) resets its modal angle memory `lastA = 0` at every tool change (`onToolChange`) and starts the program at `lastA = 0`. A tilted record at A0 then writes no A word, although the post never commanded A0 and the table may stand anywhere. Reproduced on main (f490458a) with `rotaryBrake: true`:

```
TOOL 1 T1 / SECTION / Rapid ... A 30000 / Feed ... A 30000 / ENDSECTION
TOOL 2 T2 / SECTION / Rapid ... A 0     / Feed ... A 0     / ENDSECTION
```

posts `G00 X0 Y0 Z5 A30` for the first tool, then for the second tool `G00 X0 Y0 Z5` and `G01 X0 Y0 Z0 F100` with no `A0` - the second operation cuts at A30.

**Expected:** the first A of a program, and the first A after anything that may have moved the table, is written; the modal memory is the angle the post last wrote, never an assumed 0. (The G43.4 branch is not affected - its arm writes all three words.)

PR for #885 reads the held angle only from the A words a block actually wrote, so a non-TCP feed that turns from an A the post never placed is now refused by name when the A states a rate - but with no stated rate the wrong program above still posts.

Done means: a pinning test posting the two-tool stream above writes A0 for the second tool (and an opening A0), goldens moved only where an A word was missing, each listed.

title: M12.1: a machining mesh from solidcore-tess - largest mesh-to-surface deviation benched, and every planner shortfall a refusal

labels.name: source:agent

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
What is left of point 4 of #916 (tessellation), found while benching it.

Facts from the bench (`crates/kernel/tests/step_agreement.rs`, solidcore pin `55d0e7638b9e1ebbf91ab8c10657e595c114ecda`): solidcore now has a mesher, `solidcore-tess`, which meshes the STEP reader's B-rep record at a chord tolerance in millimetres. At the app's 0.005 mm cap it is watertight on every fixture when vertices are welded by exact position (truck's per-face meshes leave 854 open triangle sides on Milling-test.step and 3196 on sample_ap214.step by the same count), and its volume and area are closer to the exact solid than truck's (5.6e-5 against 1.2e-4 relative on Milling-test). It uses more triangles (6228 against 952).

Owed before #917 can make the app's mesh with it:

1. **The deviation that matters for a gouge check is not measured yet.** The bench compares volume, area, bounding box and watertightness. It does not measure the largest distance from the mesh to the exact surface. Bench it per fixture against the chord asked for (0.005 mm, and the caps of #689 / #864), for solidcore-tess and for truck's mesh, and pin the verdicts.
2. **Its own docs call it a display mesher** ("a display mesh decides nothing a model depends on: it is drawn, never measured"), and it reports what it could not do in `PlanStats` instead of failing: `unmeshed`, `lenient` (a face filled leniently so the display has no hole), `over_tolerance`, `edges_capped`, `unsampled_edges`. A machining import must turn every one of those into a named refusal or a reduced-fidelity flag (#864 / PR #911), never a silent mesh. Decide which, per entry, and pin each with a fixture that provokes it.
3. **Triangle budget.** The app caps facets (`MAX_FACETS`) and coarsens to stay inside memory. solidcore-tess has its own bounds; state how the app's budget maps onto them.
4. **wasm32.** `solidcore-tess` gates rayon off on wasm32 in its manifest; a wasm32 check of it has not been run from this workspace.

Everything stays inside `crates/kernel` until #917 (low coupling, #919).

Part of #27. Gates #917.

Done means: the deviation bench runs in the kernel's lane with its table pinned; each `PlanStats` shortfall has a decided outcome and a test; the answer on the triangle budget and on wasm32 is a comment here.

title: M12.1: solidcore's tight bounding box takes the whole cylinder of a trimmed face (Milling-test.step: Y max 30.0, true 19.719), plus two smaller findings at pin 55d0e763

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found by the STEP bench of #916 (`crates/kernel/tests/step_agreement.rs`), at the solidcore pin `55d0e7638b9e1ebbf91ab8c10657e595c114ecda`.

**1. Wrong bounding box (the one that matters).**
`testdata/models/Milling-test.step` (and its inch twin) is a 60 mm disc with a flat at Y = 19.719. Imported through `camcraft_kernel::solidcore_step`, the solid's volume (52808.744 mm^3) and area (11143.378 mm^2) agree with truck's mesh to 1.2e-4, but `StepSolid::measure`'s box - the port's `calculate_bounding_box` with `tight: true` - is `[-30, -30, -5]..[30, 30, 20]`. The file's own vertices, truck's mesh and solidcore's own mesh (`solidcore-tess`) all stop at Y = 19.719. The box takes the whole R = 30 cylinder, not the trimmed face. It is pinned in the bench as `disagree: bounding box`.

Not known yet: whether the port's box is wrong for any trimmed periodic face, or whether the record-to-kernel build (`solidcore_convert::brep::to_kernel_body`) gives the face a parameter box that covers the whole circle. A kernel-made fixture (a cylinder cut by a plane through the seam's own booleans) would tell the two apart.

Why P1: stage 5 (#917) puts imported geometry under every toolpath. A box 10 mm too large would mis-size automatic stock and mis-place anything aligned to the part's extent.

**2. Stale cached topology after the build.** `to_kernel_body` hands out a B-rep whose cached `Face::shell` is behind its face-use links on every fixture; the port's `topology::integrity::check` refuses it ("cached face shell: face 0 not found"). The seam works around it with `Brep::refresh_cached_topology()` (public; rewrites the cached fields only). To report upstream (tangency-labs/solidcore); the maintainer decides who files it there.

**3. No cancellation in the STEP topology pass.** `solidcore_step::topology::read_solids` takes no progress or cancel hook, so the importer's time bound cannot stop it; it is bounded only by the reader's caps and the seam's 64 MiB size bound. To raise upstream, or to bound by calling the per-solid readers from the seam.

Part of #27. Gates #917.

Done means: the Milling-test rows of the bench read `agree` (the box fixed at its source, or the importer taking its box from a source that is right, with the reason recorded), the root cause is named in a decision entry, and findings 2 and 3 are either fixed at a new pin or filed upstream with their links here.

title: MCP: set WCS from feature picks

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server and agent tooling (crates/app/src/mcp, camcraft-mcp skill)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
PR #706 grew the GUI's "Set WCS from features": pick edges, vertices, faces and cylinder walls, say which axis each one sets, and the WCS lands on the fitted frame, undoable (#701). The MCP surface cannot do the equivalent. `set_wcs` (`crates/app/src/mcp/setup_tools.rs`) takes only an absolute origin or a stock-bbox point plus offset, and rotation is a raw unit quaternion - so an agent has to solve the frame maths itself from `list_features` output, and a wrong quaternion posts shifted toolpaths with no diagnostic.

The id-driven precedent already exists: `locate_part` mates part/fixture features **by `list_features` id** and fits the 3-2-1 itself; `set_operation_geometry` takes the same ids.

**Proposal:** a tool (say `set_wcs_from_features`) taking the active setup and picks as `[{id, role}]` with `role` in `origin | x | y | z`, and:

- runs the GUI's exact law - `pick::roles::align_roles` (`crates/app/src/pick/roles.rs`): Z, X, Y priority, first axis exact, second projected perpendicular, third derived to close the frame; origin anchored at the feature's natural centre; cylinder walls by covariance fit. No second frame law to drift;
- returns refusals as MCP error strings, the same named ones the GUI says: too few picks, duplicate role, fewer than two axes, parallel axes (5 degree tilt rule), zero-length edge, unresolvable datum, stale feature id;
- queues the existing `CommandKind::SetWcs` - no new command kind, one undoable step. The "commands ship with an MCP tool" rule is satisfied by the tool itself (as noted on #706).

Filed at the reviewer's suggestion in the #706 review (https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/pull/706): keep the agent surface level with the GUI. Related: #701, #709.

title: Build cache: skills and agents say how to use sccache for direct cargo calls; the release build clears the wrapper

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
PR #913 (PROCESS_VERSION 15) made `cargo xtask gate` use sccache by itself, but a plain `cargo test -p ...`, `cargo build` or `cargo clippy` only uses the cache when `RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache` is set in the shell, and nothing tells the agents so: the skills only say not to export `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. Workers and reviewers that call cargo directly therefore build without the cache. Maintainer decision (2026-11-11): put the instruction in the shared files, and keep the release build out of the cache.

Do:
1. One short, identical line in `.claude/skills/work-issue/SKILL.md`, `.claude/skills/resolve-conflicts/SKILL.md`, `.claude/agents/PR-reviewer.md`, `.claude/agents/gate-runner.md` (and the `issue-worker-*` agents only if they carry build instructions of their own): prefer `cargo xtask gate ...` (it turns the cache on); for a direct cargo call, set `RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache` when `sccache` is on PATH (`command -v sccache`), never when it is not (cargo fails if the wrapper is missing); never export `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. AGENTS.md's build-cache paragraph says the same in one sentence.
2. `cargo xtask release` (`xtask/src/release.rs`, `build()`) builds the shipped binary WITHOUT a compiler wrapper even when `RUSTC_WRAPPER` is set in the environment (remove it from the child's environment), pinned by an xtask unit test. Reason: a maintainer may set `RUSTC_WRAPPER` machine-wide (this repo's maintainer has, in local Claude Code settings), and the released artifact must not depend on a compile cache. The release GATE tier may keep using the cache; only the packaging build clears it - say so in the code comment.
3. Do NOT add `rustc-wrapper` to the checked-in `.cargo/config.toml` (cargo fails outright on a machine without sccache) and do not add it to the checked-in `.claude/settings.json` for the same reason.

Process files: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` (16, or the next free number when it merges); the merge is announced on #681.

Done means: the four files carry the line; AGENTS.md matches; the release packaging build ignores `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, pinned by a unit test; xtask's unit tests pass. Related: #900, #914, #915.

title: Work offsets: core uses an index, the post supplies the word and display name

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server and agent tooling (crates/app/src/mcp, camcraft-mcp skill)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
## Problem

A setup stores its work offset as an index (`SetupDef::work_offset`), but core
turns that index into a Fanuc-style word before any post is involved:

- The table `WCS_SLOTS = ["G54".."G59"]` lives in `camcraft-app`
  (`operation/types/sel.rs`) and is read directly by the Setups page combo,
  `setup::wcs_label`, the setup sheet, the MCP `set_work_offset` tool and the
  refusal messages.
- `posting::wcs_context` writes the word, not the index, into the stream as
  `PARAM WorkOffset`. Posts then parse it back: Fanuc and Mazak use
  `slotOf("G55") -> 1`, Heidenhain regex-matches `^G5([4-9])$` to pick a preset
  row.
- An index of 6 or more is refused in core, so extended offsets
  (`G54.1 P..`, Sinumerik `G505+`, further Heidenhain preset rows) cannot be
  expressed.

A setup with no machine and no post still shows `G54`: the word comes from
neither. Every other ask in the stream is already dialect-neutral (coolant,
after-operation); the work offset is the exception.

## Proposal

1. **Stream carries the index.** `PARAM WorkOffset` becomes a 1-based number.
   A manifest flag (`workOffsetIndex = true`) opts a script in, following the
   `coolantModes` / `afterModes` pattern. A script without the flag keeps
   receiving the word for offsets 1-6, so user-loaded posts keep working, and
   is refused by setup name for any offset above 6.
2. **Each post maps the index to its own word** and refuses, by setup name,
   an index it cannot express. The limit becomes the post's, not core's.
3. **The post supplies the display name.** A script may define a function
   (for example `workOffsetName(n)`) returning what the control calls offset
   `n` ("G55", "G54.1 P3", "preset 2"). The UI, setup sheet, MCP tool and
   refusal messages show "WCS n (name)" for the setup's resolved post.
4. **Fallback.** A script that defines no name function shows plain "WCS n".
5. **Core and UI speak indexes.** `WCS_SLOTS` leaves `camcraft-app` and
   `camcraft-ui`, apart from the two pre-v54 file migrations that need the old
   words to read old files.

## Out of scope

- The project file format: it already stores the index, so no version step.
- The legacy `G54` entity name of a document without setups (internal name
  only; renaming it would need a migration for no user benefit).
- Rotated work offsets (#315, #760).

## Open questions

- Where the name lookup lives so the layering holds (ui -> app -> post): an
  app-level function that evaluates the setup's post, with caching, since the
  UI must not evaluate scripts per frame.
- The MCP tool's input: accept an index, and keep accepting the old words as
  aliases for 1-6?
- Whether the six-offset cap is replaced by a per-post maximum the script
  declares, so the combo can list the right number of entries.
- Whether the simulator or any test harness parses the posted offset word
  back; not yet checked.

## Acceptance

- Every existing posted-program golden is byte-identical (the 148 that
  contain a `G5x` word included).
- Every shipped `.cps` declares the flag and maps the index itself; no
  `slotOf`-style parsing of a word remains.
- A setup can be given offset 7 or higher and posts correctly on a dialect
  that supports it; a dialect that does not refuses by setup name.
- A user post without the flag posts offsets 1-6 exactly as before.
- The Setups page shows the resolved post's name for each offset, and
  "WCS n" when the post supplies none.
- `docs/CNC-INTERMEDIATE.md` and `assets/posts/AGENTS.md` describe the new
  value, flag and name function.

## Related

Background (closed):

- #196 and #342 introduced the current design: G54-G59 is the setup's post
  label.
- #51 added Heidenhain preset selection for other work offsets - the source
  of the `G5x` -> preset-row regex.
- #876 already called "work offset word" jargon in the UI.

Open work this touches:

- #836 (TinyG post) and #728 (Sienci AltMill on the grblHAL post) add new
  `.cps` files that would need the flag and the mapping.
- #258 (Post dialog) touches the same post-options area.
- #760 (rotated work offset) touches the WCS code; rotation stays out of
  scope here.

Maintainer direction (2026-11-11): "We should aim for a high cohesion low coupling thru out our codebase as we are built crates and tests. And every gate is very costly."

Where the cost comes from today (measured 2026-11-11 on main 0e36fd14):

| Crate | Source lines | Test files (one binary each) | Depends on (workspace) |
|---|---|---|---|
| app | 72,122 | 267 | cl, geometry, motion, post, sim, tools |
| ui | 57,060 | 14 | app |
| motion | 46,643 | 65 | cl, geometry, sim, tools |
| sim | 23,444 | 50 | cl, geometry, tools |
| post | 6,181 | 5 | cl, geometry |
| geometry | 5,539 | 4 | - |
| tools | 4,306 | 1 | - |
| cl | 3,723 | 1 | - |
| kernel | 1,185 | 5 | - |

- `app` is the hub: it depends on every domain crate, so almost any change rebuilds it, and each of its 267 test files links the whole crate into its own binary.
- Tests of one domain's behaviour live in `app` (post dialect tests such as `fanuc_post`, `tormach_post`, `heidenhain_*` sit in `crates/app/tests/` while `crates/post/tests/` has 5 files), so a post-only change still builds and links `app`.
- A geometry / cl / Cargo change falls back to the batch tier.
- Each worktree's `target/` is 25-56 GB; five builds at once took the disk from 166 GB to 13 GB free on 2026-11-11.

Open questions to answer here (research, no code):
1. Fan-out: for a change in each crate, which crates and how many test binaries rebuild and relink, and how long does it take (cold and warm, with #913's cache)? One table.
2. Test placement: which `crates/app/tests/*` files test behaviour owned by post, sim, motion, cl, tools or geometry and could move to that crate with a small fixture seam instead of the whole app? Count per target crate.
3. Test binaries: what does folding a crate's test files into a few binaries (one per gate-map group) save in link time and disk, and what does it cost (`gate test <name>` selection, parallel runs, the quick tier's changed-test picking in `xtask/src/plan.rs`)?
4. Coupling: which `app` modules could become their own crate (the M4.1 seams still inside `app`: operation, project, commands, mcp, machine), and which dependencies between domain crates could be cut or inverted (motion -> sim; the new post -> tools from PR #880)?
5. Rules: which of this becomes law in AGENTS.md "Code shape" and a reviewer check (e.g. a test lives in the crate that owns the behaviour; a new dependency between workspace crates needs a decision entry; no new test file in `app` for behaviour another crate owns)?

Then file the concrete sub-issues (each with P*, effort, area, "Done means", "Part of #<this>"), ordered by gate minutes saved per unit of work, and close this umbrella.

Found while working #864 (a STEP model imported coarser than the importer promises is flagged, its gouge verdicts tightened, and refused past that).

**What #864's PR does.** A reduced-fidelity model carries its achieved error. The gouge laws of the upright mill kinds subtract the excess from their tolerance while a positive tolerance is left: the section law (b), the solid law (b2), the envelope law's gouge half (f), `generate::contain_into`, the lathe's axial hole verdict, and the program sim's deviation tolerance. Past that, the program gate refuses by name.

**What is owed.** Everything below is safe today (refused, or stricter than before), but less useful than it should be.

1. **Kinds refused outright on any reduced-fidelity model**, because their gouge laws do not read the excess yet (`operation::fidelity_law::excess_aware`):
   - the cone and engrave rides: 2D chamfer, deburr, trace, engrave (generator construction laws);
   - probe, and the cross drill (`operation/cross_part.rs`, `SolidLaw { allow: GOUGE_TOL }`);
   - the multi-axis kinds (`motion` `multiaxis/entry_ramp.rs`, `stamp*.rs`, `rotary_links.rs`) and the rotary kinds (`operation/rotary_law.rs`, `allow` and `rapid_allow`);
   - turning (`motion` `turning/revolve.rs`, `form.rs`, `thread.rs`; `blade_warnings`, `thread_warnings`, `form_warnings`);
   - plasma.
   Each needs `material.excess` threaded into its law and the kind added to `excess_aware`. A metre-unit STEP file is always reduced fidelity (next point), so these kinds cannot post on one today.
2. **Collision laws are not tightened**: shank and holder reach (`sim` `verify/reach.rs`), rapids in stock (`verify/rapids.rs`, `rapids_posed.rs`, `rapids_radial.rs`), the turning rapid, bar-feed and holder scans (`margin: GOUGE_TOL` in `generate.rs`). 4. **The facet budget is not a user setting.** The refusal says "re-import with a larger budget" (the maintainer's wording on #864), but `MAX_FACETS` is a constant. The import dialog, the script verb and MCP `import_model` need a budget the user can raise.
5. **Display tolerances** still read the plain 0.01 mm on a reduced-fidelity model: the machined-surface classes (`machined_classes.rs`) and the viewport preview (`ui` `trace/eye.rs`, `cpu_eye.rs`). The binding verdict is tightened; the colours are not.
6. **The envelope law (f) and the containment solid law** are tightened through the same helper as (b) but have no fixture-level pin of their own on a reduced-fidelity model.

title: Build cycle: every worktree compiles the whole dependency tree cold - share a compile cache, cut debug info, use a faster linker

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
Raised by the maintainer (2026-11-11): "why are we cold building complete bundles .. the tests are localized to crates".

## What happens today (measured on the dev machine)
- Every issue worker, reviewer and gate works in its own worktree with its own `target/`. A fresh one compiles the WHOLE dependency tree before the first test runs: about 15-25 minutes per review and 25-75 minutes per gate, almost all of it third-party crates (flecs' C through bindgen/cc, wgpu/egui, the B-rep kernel, the script engine ...), not our code.
- `Cargo.toml` sets `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2`: every dependency is optimised in dev builds. That makes tests run faster but makes each cold build much slower.
- Nothing sets `debug`, so dev builds carry full debug info for all crates: one `target/` reaches 50-120 GB (the disk filled twice today) and every link is slow.
- Integration tests are one binary per file: `crates/app/tests` has 266 files, motion 65, sim 50. The batch gate's app step takes about 24 of its 38 minutes, much of it linking and starting 266 binaries.
- `.cargo/config.toml` holds only the `xtask` alias: no linker choice, no cache wrapper. `sccache` is not installed; `rust-lld` is.

## Wanted (this issue: the three cheap ones, measured)
1. **A shared compile cache across worktrees** (`sccache` as `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and as the C compiler wrapper for the cc-built C code if that works on MSVC). Registry crates live at the same path for every worktree, so their compilations are cache hits; a fresh worktree should then compile only our own crates. It must be OPTIONAL: a machine without sccache builds exactly as today (enable it from `cargo xtask` / the gate wrappers when `sccache` is on PATH, or document the env var - never hard-code a wrapper in `.cargo/config.toml` that breaks a machine without it). Say how to install it and how big its cache is allowed to grow.
2. **Less debug info**: `debug = false` (or `"line-tables-only"`) for dependencies, and line tables only for our crates in dev/test - enough for backtraces and panics with file:line. Report target size and link time before/after.
3. **A faster linker** for the Windows MSVC target (`rust-lld` / `lld-link`), and the equivalent on Linux/macOS where it helps, again without breaking a machine that lacks it.
4. Re-examine `opt-level = 2` for all dependencies: keep it only for the crates whose speed the tests need (measure: batch gate time with opt-level 2 everywhere vs 1 vs a short list).

Measure and report, on the same machine, cold (empty target, warm cache where a cache applies) and warm: `cargo test -p camcraft-app --no-run`, `cargo test -p camcraft-app --test <one binary>`, `cargo xtask gate quick` on a one-file app change, and the `target/` size. No test may change behaviour; the gates stay green.

## Not in this issue (file separately if the numbers say so)
- Folding the 266 one-file app test binaries into a few binaries (one per area, files as modules). This is the biggest structural win for the gate, but it changes the gate maps in `xtask` and every "run this binary" instruction.

## Process
`.cargo/config.toml`, `xtask/` and the gate wrappers are process files: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, and say in the PR what a fork must do.

Done means: a fresh worktree reaches its first app test at least 3x faster than today with the cache warm, `target/` is at most half today's size, the settings are optional per machine and documented, and the measured numbers are in the PR.

title: STEP import refuses a valid HOOPS Exchange file: ruststep cannot parse an empty parameter list `()` — one entity kills the whole DATA section, and the error points at the wrong line

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
## What happens

Opening `4B52391_step_conversion_r_0.step` (16.5 KB, exported by HOOPS Exchange 2026.7) in CamCraft v0.17.0 fails with:

```text
corrupt STEP: syntax error: Error while tokenizing STEP input

0: at line 20, in Tag:
DATA;
^
```

Other STEP readers open the file without complaint (SolidCraft among them). The part is a plain `ADVANCED_BREP / MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP / CLOSED_SHELL` with 13 faces — nothing exotic.

The error is also misleading: line 20 is just the `DATA;` keyword line. Delete the HOOPS comment from the header and the error "moves" to line 18 — it always lands on `DATA;`, which never misled *me* to the header. The real defect is deep inside the DATA section, at entity `#11` (line 435):

```step
#11=DRAUGHTING_MODEL('',(),#10);
```

## Reproduction

1. Get a STEP file exported by HOOPS Exchange (a very common commercial SDK; lots of cloud converters route through it) — or use the 9-line file below.
2. `File → Open` in CamCraft, or call `camcraft_app::geometry::import::load_model` headless.
3. Expected: the part loads. Actual: `corrupt STEP: syntax error … at line 20, in Tag: DATA;`.

Minimal repro (a whole valid STEP file — this reproduces the exact symptom):

```step
ISO-10303-21;
HEADER;
FILE_DESCRIPTION(('test'),'2;1');
FILE_NAME('repro','2026-11-11T00:00:00','','');
FILE_SCHEMA(('AUTOMOTIVE_DESIGN'));
ENDSEC;
DATA;
#1=A('',(),#2);
ENDSEC;
END-ISO-10303-21;
```

Remove the `()` from `#1` and it loads. That one construct is the whole bug.

## Root cause — an upstream ruststep bug, not a bad file

ISO 10303-21 defines `list = "(" [ parameter { "," parameter } ] ")"` — the empty list `()` is legal. ruststep 0.4.0 (the latest release, Sep 2024) parses lists with `list()` → `comma_separated(parameter)`, and its `separated` combinator is `tuple((f, many0(sep+f)))` — **at least one element required**. So `()` never parses, anywhere.

- Upstream status: [ricosjp/ruststep#256](https://github.com/ricosjp/ruststep/issues/256) (open, filed Feb 2026) reports the same bug against the released crate. The fix is *already on upstream main* — [`90fdc935` "fix(exchange): handle empty parameter lists"](https://github.com/ricosjp/ruststep/commit/90fdc9351746f1f1d1e435b88f15371edaaaa14d) (Feb 2025) wraps the element list in `opt_(...)` and adds an `empty_parameter_list` test — but it has never shipped: the newest crates.io release is still 0.4.0 (Sep 2024), which predates it. So the one-line fix exists; it just needs a pin.
- Why the error message is wrong: `entity_instance_list` is `many0_(entity_instance)`, so parsing silently *stops* at `#11`; then the `ENDSEC;` tag fails, `data_section` fails, and the outer `many0_(data_section)` in `exchange_file` **discards that failure and yields zero sections** — the last error nom keeps is the `END-ISO-10303-21;` tag check, which lands on `DATA;`. Hence "line 20".

Bisection evidence (v0.17.0 code paths, headless):

| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| original file | `corrupt STEP … at line 20, in Tag: DATA;` |
| header comment removed | same failure, now "line 18" — header is innocent |
| `#11`'s `()` replaced by `(#10)` | **loads fine — 164 facets** |
| 9-line minimal repro with `()` | fails with the identical wrong-line symptom |

Roughly 400 of the file's 416 DATA entities use no empty lists; the single `DRAUGHTING_MODEL('',(),#10)` — an entity that isn't even geometry — is enough to reject the entire part.

## Proposed fixes (not exclusive)

1. **Short term, smallest real fix:** `[patch.crates-io]` ruststep to an upstream git rev that includes [`90fdc935`](https://github.com/ricosjp/ruststep/commit/90fdc9351746f1f1d1e435b88f15371edaaaa14d) (upstream main still declares `version = "0.4.0"`, so CamCraft's direct dep *and* truck-stepio's `ruststep = "0.4"` both resolve to the patched crate unchanged; pin a `rev`/`tag` for reproducibility). If a git dependency is not wanted, the fallback is a small fork + `[patch.crates-io]`, or preprocessing `()` — but that's text-hacking around a parser bug. Bonus either way: pin the 9-line repro (or the real file) as a regression test asset so whichever route taken can't silently regress when ruststep finally releases.
2. **Error UX regardless:** when STEP import fails, say *where parsing stopped* (entity `#11` here) rather than a line number in the header, and say the file may well be valid — currently "corrupt STEP" sends users to re-export blindly. Since ruststep's `VerboseError` swallows the inner failure, even a cheap second pass ("re-parse entity by entity to find the first failing one") would beat today's message.
3. **Long term:** #27 (Solidcore replaces the B-rep engine) makes the whole ruststep/truck-stack class of import failures go away — this is one more data point for why that milestone matters.

(I've kept the original failing file offline since it contains my part geometry — happy to share it with a maintainer privately if that helps; the 9-line repro above reproduces the identical failure.)

body:
Found while reworking #850 (PR #865).

**What happens:** app `pocket3d_hsm::the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean` (heavy lane, `testdata/models/Milling-test.step`). On main, one level's growth plan spends **~200 s in release** in `adaptive/grow.rs`: 33 revolutions, 157 trial steps, about 1.3 s per trial.

**Where the time goes** (local probe, release):
- 99 % of it is `rings::open`, the morphological opening: two `offset_fine` calls at `ARC_TOL` 2.5e-4 mm per trial, plus one per revolution for `whole`.
- The stock walk takes 0.6 s.
- The cleared-area offset and the intersect take 0.2 s each.

The opening's cost grows about with the **square** of the ring's vertex count. Measured cost per (vertices per trial)^2:

| fixture | vertices per trial | ns per (vertices)^2 |
|---|---|---|
| 60 x 14 slot | ~290 | ~63 |
| 60 x 40 island | ~700 | ~105 |
| the bore (fine STEP tessellation) | ~4,700 | ~58 |

So a finely tessellated outline turns a 33-revolution plan into minutes.

**Why it is not bounded:** #850's budget cannot refuse it without changing a plan that finishes on main. Measured on any time-faithful unit, the bore is the most expensive plan of all, so it stays law 2's (length) alone. See `docs/decisions/850-adaptive-geometry-budget.md`.

**Options:**
- Simplify the cleared area and the ring to the planner's working tolerance before the opening. Douglas-Peucker at the `MERGE` / `ARC_TOL` scale would remove the boolean engine's arc-tolerance vertices that say nothing about the shape.
- An opening that does not re-tessellate every convex vertex at `ARC_TOL`.
- An incremental opening.

Each option changes toolpaths: under the safety floor, with every adaptive fixture re-measured.

**Done means:** the bore's growth level plans in seconds (stated bound, release and debug) with the load, crossing and kink laws held. Every adaptive fixture's change is measured and named in the PR.

title: Theme and colour-vision mode are user preferences, not project state: remember them per user

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
**What happens now**

The theme is document state. `SetTheme` writes a `ThemeRef` singleton into the world, the project file saves it as an optional `theme` key (`crates/app/src/project/file.rs`, written by `project/wire.rs`), and opening a project sets it again (`project/apply.rs`; no key means Dark). So:

- A new document always opens in Dark.
- Each project carries its own theme. Someone who works in Light has to switch every new project, and a colleague's project opens in whatever theme its author used.
- Changing the theme is an undoable edit to the document, and it marks the project as changed.

**Decision (reporter, vilts, 2026-11-11):** the theme and the colour-vision mode are purely user preferences. They have nothing to do with the project, and both survive program restarts.

**Proposed**

- Keep the chosen theme per user, in the OS config folder, the same way recent files already do (#662, `app::recent`: `%APPDATA%`, `~/Library/Application Support`, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`; write to a temp file, then rename; a missing or corrupt file starts at the default and says why on the status line, never crashes). Read it at startup and write it when the user picks a theme.
- The project file stops storing the theme. Saving writes no `theme` key. Opening ignores a `theme` key in older files and leaves the user's theme as it is (a compatible read, so no project-file version break is needed for existing documents). Opening a project or File > New never changes the look.
- A missing theme file (a `{"file": path}` preference whose file is gone) keeps the current behaviour: refused by name on the status line, falling back to the built-in default without crashing.
- Theme selection leaves the document's undo history, like the recent-files list (#662: "app PREFERENCE state, not document state"). The pick still goes through one place that validates it (the existing pre-parse in `State::select_theme`), so a corrupt theme is refused at the pick.

**Colour-vision mode too**

The colour-vision mode (`SetColorVision`) is not in the project file and is not saved anywhere, so it resets on every restart. It is kept in the same per-user preference store as the theme, read at startup, and written when the user picks a mode. The startup read still runs the colour-vision gate against the theme it lands on, so a stored mode that fails the gate is refused by name, not applied silently.

**Tests**

The existing theme tests pin the old design and are removed, not updated:
- `project_roundtrip.rs::the_theme_choice_round_trips_and_a_v40_file_means_dark` (the save writes `theme`, and opening applies it)
- `commands_undo.rs::theme_choice_undoes_redoes_and_refuses` (a pick is in the undo history)

Replaced by:
- One project-file test of the new rule: saving writes no `theme` key, and opening an older file that still carries `"theme": {...}` loads cleanly and leaves the user's theme as it was. This guards against a project file overriding the preference again.
- Preference-store tests for theme and colour vision: survives a restart, and a missing or corrupt file starts at the default with a note.

**Done means**

Pick Light, then File > New: the new document is Light. Open a project saved with `"theme": {"named": "dark"}`: it stays Light. Restart the app: still Light. Pick a colour-vision mode, restart: still that mode. Saving a project writes no `theme` key. A corrupt preference file starts in Dark with a status-line note. Tests pin each of these, with the preference store pointed at a temp folder so the suites never touch the real user file.

Labels intended (the filer can't set labels): `enhancement`, `P2`, `effort:medium`, `area:ui`, `source:agent`. Related: #662 (recent files, the store to copy), #698 (light theme), #659.

labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:low
labels.description: Mechanical, one file, no new logic (issue-worker-low)

body:
Reported by the maintainer from the properties panel (2026-11-11), investigated and filed by an agent.

## What the user sees
On the WCS node's page:

```
WCS (G54): 52.80, -128.60, 5.00  yaw 0.0
The work offset word is set per setup on the Setups page.
  Work offset  [G54 v]
```

The sentence sends the user to another page for a setting whose dropdown sits on the very next line. And "work offset word" reads as nonsense unless you know that RS-274 calls `G54` a "word".

## Is it invented text? No - it is real text that went stale
- `crates/ui/src/egui_app/pages.rs:648` draws the sentence at the end of `wcs_page`. It came with #342 (commit 6e8deca9, "one WCS per setup; G54-G59 is only the setup's post label"); the code comment above it says the word "is chosen on the Setups page, never here". That was true then.
- #343 then added the picker to this same page: `pages.rs:143-148` calls `wcs_page(ui, state)` and, right after a separator, `setup_wcs_pick::picker(ui, state, name)` ("the WCS node's dialog names its post word too"). The sentence was not removed, so the page now contradicts itself.
- The setting itself is sound: the dropdown queues the undoable `SetSetupWorkOffset`, and the post reads the word through `setup::wcs_slot` (one source). Nothing is wrong with the output; only the text is.

## The same jargon elsewhere
- `crates/ui/src/egui_app/heights_page.rs:108-109` `SETUP_OFFSET_HINT`: "program zero is the setup's WCS: its work offset word is set on the Setups page" (hover on the read-only Work offset row of an operation's heights). True there - that row has no dropdown - but the wording is the same jargon, and since #343 the setting is on the WCS page as well as the Setups page.
- The picker's own hover (`setup_wcs_pick.rs`) says "The G-word the post writes for this setup's WCS ..." - accurate, same jargon.

## Fix
1. Remove the stale sentence from `wcs_page` (and correct the comment above it), or replace it with one line that is true on this page, e.g. "Work offset: the G54-G59 register this setup posts. It does not move the origin."
2. Say "work offset (G54-G59)" instead of "work offset word" / "G-word" in user-facing text: the WCS page, `SETUP_OFFSET_HINT`, the picker's hover. Where a hint points elsewhere, it names the places that really have the control (the WCS page and the Setups page).
3. Sweep the UI strings once for other "... is set on the X page" hints and check each still points at a page that has the control; list what was checked in the PR.
4. Update the structural/AccessKit assertions that pin these strings (`setup_wcs_tests`, `one_wcs`, heights page tests) - no snapshot PNG changes.

Done means: no page tells the user to go elsewhere for a control it shows itself; no user-facing string says "work offset word" or "G-word"; the tests that pin the strings are updated; no behaviour, command or posted output changes.

Part of #866.

**Root cause:** the native file dialogs (`crates/ui/src/file_dialog.rs`, rfd) are modal and synchronous, and they are opened from `State::drain_actions`, inside the frame's "commands" phase (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/shell_window/frame.rs`). title: Coolant: the machine editor drops an added Air M7, the Carvera post emits M8 from the seeded Flood, and operations can't ask for air

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
From the same Makera Z1 user report (2026-11-11). Makera machines cool with **air, M7**. The user built a Z1 machine file in the editor and tried to add M7 air cooling: **"this was ignored when I saved the profile"**. They asked to be able to:
- disable the default (flood) cooling in the editor and swap it for air; or
- keep both in the profile and choose one per operation.

**What we know from the code (main):**
- A new machine draft is seeded with `"coolants": [{ "name": "Flood", "mCode": "M8" }]` (`crates/app/src/machine/draft.rs:91`).
- `add_coolant` adds a name with **no code** (`draft.rs:147-165`). A coolant whose code is never filled in may then be skipped or dropped. That's likely the "ignored on save".
- `carvera.cps` `coolantCode()` returns the **first `Flood` entry**, else the first entry with a code. So a profile still holding the seeded Flood M8 posts **M8**, even after an Air M7 is added. On a Makera that's the wrong M-code: M8 isn't the air blast.
- Operations choose `CoolantMode` Off / Flood / Mist / Through tool (`crates/post/src/post/coolant.rs`). There's no **Air** mode, and Flood is the silent default, so an op can't ask for "air" by name. The generic posts look the word up in the machine's list and refuse by name when it's missing.

**Fix (sketch; the worker decides the details and records them):**
1. **The editor** can remove or replace the seeded Flood entry, and an added coolant gets its code entered before it's saved. A save never silently drops a coolant; it's refused by name if one is incomplete.
2. **An `Air` coolant mode** (or "air blast", M7 on Makera), selectable per operation, which the posts resolve from the machine's list like Mist.
3. **A machine-level default coolant**, so a machine whose only coolant is air defaults new operations to Air, not Flood.
4. **`carvera.cps`** posts the coolant the operation asked for, not "first Flood". If the machine has no matching entry, it's a named refusal, never a wrong M-code.

Effort: high: it changes posted G-code (safety floor).

**Done means:**
- a machine file with only Air M7 posts M7/M9 for a default operation;
- a profile edited in the GUI keeps its Air M7 after save and reload;
- an operation asking for a coolant the machine lacks is refused by name;
- all pinned.

title: An over-budget STEP mesh is imported at reduced fidelity with only a log line - gouge verdicts on it can pass a real gouge on a convex wall

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
Found in the review of PR #839 (#689).

**What happens.** `crates/app/src/geometry/import/step.rs` (`shell_facets`, the refinement loop and the `eprintln!` at about lines 188-207) refines a STEP shell toward its chord target. Since #689 that target is `min(extent/1000, 0.005 mm)`. Refinement stops early once the mesh passes `budget / 8` facets (`MAX_FACETS` = 30 M, less what earlier shells used), or when a pass returns `TooLarge`. The importer then keeps the coarser mesh and only prints "step: tessellated at reduced fidelity ..." to stderr. Nothing in the model, the UI, MCP or the program gate records that the mesh is coarser than the gouge verdict assumes.

A related wrinkle: on the `Err(TooLarge) => break` path, `tol` has already been halved while `refined` is the previous, coarser mesh. The log then under-reports the chord error, and if the halved `tol` reaches the target, it says nothing at all.

**Why it matters, in both directions.** The gouge laws judge the program against these facets with a 0.01 mm verdict. A facet is a chord inscribed in the true surface, so it stands inside the material by its sagitta. That cuts both ways:

- **Concave wall** (a bore or a pocket wall): the facets stand toward the tool. A nominal finish reads as a false gouge, which is the safe side. This was the #689 symptom.
- **Convex wall** (a boss or an outside profile): the facets stand away from the tool, so the mesh wall looks farther off than the real wall. A real gouge up to the mesh's actual chord error can pass the verdict. This is the unsafe side.

AGENTS.md, Prime Directive: "if an operation can only be partly computed, mark it 'incomplete' rather than emit a subtly wrong toolpath", and "Log diagnostics, never silence". A stderr line the user never sees is silence.

This risk is not new. Before #689 every STEP mesh was made at `extent/1000`, which is never finer than what an over-budget model gets now. #689 removes the risk for every model that fits the budget. For an over-budget model it remains.

**Options.**
- (a) The import records the chord error it actually achieved on the model, and the gouge laws tighten their floor by the excess over the 0.005 mm cap for that model. That is stricter, never looser; false gouges on concave walls are the safe side.
- (b) The model is flagged "reduced fidelity" visibly in the UI and MCP. The program gate refuses to post operations judged against it until the user acknowledges it or re-imports with a larger budget.
- (c) Both.

**Recommended: (c).** (a) alone keeps the verdict sound but leaves the user wondering about false gouges. (b) alone relies on an acknowledgement.

Done means: an over-budget import is visible to the user and to MCP; no gouge verdict on such a model can be looser than on a full-fidelity one; and tests pin both, including the `TooLarge`-break path's reported chord error.

title: adaptive growth: the overload fallback picks the largest step on truncated readings and walks it far past the bound

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
What happens: `Planner::step_search` (crates/motion/src/machining2d/adaptive/grow.rs) tries up to 7 growth steps with `walk_until(.., limit = bound)`, which stops at the FIRST reading past the bound. When no step holds, the fallback keeps "the least overload" from those truncated readings. Where the overload sits before the g-dependent front (it does not grow with the step), every try reads the same, the tie goes to the first (largest) step, and that step is then walked whole - far past the reading it was chosen on.

Evidence (release, `HSM_ONE=island hsm_one`, island 60x40/12x12, on d1920031 with the #844 compile break stubbed locally and the growth budget lifted to reach the growth): round the island's NE corner, revs 153-159 read the same first exceedance at every step from 1.88 down to 0.088 mm (e.g. rev 159: 59.5 deg x7), the largest step was kept and walked whole at 57.5 -> 125 deg (79.4 % D at (43.66, 25.81)). This is the 125 deg / 176 breaks round 9 of #7 blamed on the spiral's geometry.

Held fix: branch `issue/7-r10-corner-reading`, e4039ef0 - re-walk each tried step whole and keep the least. Island readings with it: every overloaded revolution reads <= 55 deg (bound ~47.5; worst now at the SW wall, (17.58, 6.01)), the NE-corner overloads are gone. Cost: the growth work on the island doubles (61,971 r, vs ~31,000 before, vs the #13 `WORK_MAX` 30,000), because the smaller steps take more revolutions, and each overloaded revolution adds up to 7 whole walks.

Done means: the fallback chooses the least overload by whole readings (a pinning test where the truncated reading ties and the whole reading does not), with the #13 growth budget kept honest (either the extra walks are not charged as growth work, the re-walk is bounded, or WORK_MAX is recalibrated on the fixtures with the band refusal re-timed); goldens that move are listed.

Found while working #7 (round 10). Part of the #7 picture, but a defect on any growth plan with an overloaded revolution.

title: A tool body is judged as two different shapes: the fixture laws sweep its band stack, the reach laws its enclosing cylinder - the simulation can only draw one

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while working #743 part 1 (the simulation draws the tool as the revolved outline the laws judge).

**What happens.** A milling tool with a body (an imported mesh, #368, or a drawn spun holder, #93) is read by the collision laws in two different shapes:

- the fixture laws (`fixture_struck`, `operation::generate` -> `tool_body::stack` -> `verify::steel_stack`) sweep the body's **band stack** - its revolved envelope, up to 32 coaxial bands;
- every law that reads one holder cylinder off `ToolGeom` - law (c), the shank/holder reach against the part and stock walls in `crates/sim/src/verify/reach.rs` (`cx.tool.holder_radius`, `cx.tool.holder_len`), and the probe stack in `verify/probe.rs` - reads the tool `tool_body::judged` returns: the single cylinder **enclosing** the body (`HolderProfile::enclose`): the holder at the body's widest radius from the shank top to the body's top, and the shank widened to the widest the body reaches beside it.

Both are conservative (never smaller than the body), so no collision is missed. But they are not the same shape: for a stepped body (a narrow nose under a wide flange) the enclosing cylinder is the flange's radius all the way down to the shank top.

**Why it matters.** #743 asks that the simulated tool be "the same profile the collision laws judge, so what you see is what is checked". The simulation (PR for #743 part 1) draws the band stack, the tighter of the two and the one the laws that name a fixture collision read. A reach warning from law (c) can therefore fire where the drawn holder is visibly clear of the wall: the user sees a nose 15 mm from the axis, the law judged 40 mm.

**Evidence.** `crates/app/src/tool_body.rs` (`judged`, `stack`), `crates/tools/src/holder_profile.rs` (`enclose`, `stack`), `crates/sim/src/verify/reach.rs` lines 38-45. `crates/app/tests/tool_spun_profile.rs` already pins the two readings side by side (the enclosing cylinder's radius equals the widest band).

**Options (not decided here).**
1. Law (c) and the other single-cylinder laws read the band stack too (changes verdicts: fewer false reach warnings; under the safety floor, needs its own goldens).
2. Keep the laws; a reach warning from an enclosed body says so in its text ("judged by the cylinder enclosing the body, Ø…"), and the simulation can show that cylinder when such a warning is selected.

Not touched by #743 part 1 - that PR is display only and changes no verdict.

Done means: either every law that judges a tool body reads the same shape the simulation draws (with tests pinning the changed verdicts), or the difference is stated in the warning text and shown on demand, with a test that the drawn shape and the named judged shape agree for each law.

Part of #743.

body:
Found while working #785.

The machine check (`crates/app/src/machine/mod.rs`, the pose branch of the limit judge) judges a tilted move's **letters** from `cl::axis_to_angles`. It does no IK, by design.

A 3+2 tilt stores canonical letters (A in -90..90), so the face underneath a bar arrives as **A0 B180**. On a machine whose only rotary is an **A about X** (the new `Tormach 770MX + microARC 4`), the check refuses it: "commands B 180.000 deg; ... states no B axis". Yet that A reaches the pose as A180, and the Tormach post (#785) already reads the pose through the tool axis and posts it as `G0 A180`.

So today a 4th-axis job can't cut the face at 180 degrees. It has to use the opposite pair A-90 / A90 (the #785 test part does).

**Done means:** on a machine stating one rotary about X, the check accepts any tool axis with no X component and judges its angle about X against that rotary's travel. Every other pose is still refused by name. Pinned by a test that posts an A0 B180 Slot on the 770MX + microARC 4.

title: Picking: only feature edges, feature points and faces are pickable, never tessellation edges or hidden geometry - one rule for the whole app

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Reported by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-10.

## What happens
1. **Tessellation edges are pickable.** The selector lets you pick edges between the mesh's own triangles (at a model's vertices, inside flat faces and along smooth curves). Those aren't real model edges, and no feature should ever be built on them.
2. **Picks go through the model.** In some cases, the "select through" behaviour picks an edge (or a vertex) on the far side of the model, hidden from the user, instead of what's under the cursor.
3. **Inconsistent everywhere.** Face, vertex and edge picking behave differently from page to page: setup alignment, operation geometry, fixture mates, the WCS/origin picks, MCP picks. Users can't build a mental model of what a click will select.

## What should happen - one picking rule, used everywhere
- **Faces:** a face is a welded face, i.e. a smooth patch of triangles merged across soft edges (the `features`/`area` patches MCP's `list_features` already reports). Clicking anywhere on it picks the whole face, never a single triangle.
- **Edges:** only **feature edges** are pickable: edges where two welded faces meet at a real crease, plus open boundary edges of a sheet. Edges between triangles of the same welded face (flat-face triangulation, facets of a smooth cylinder) are never pickable. Chains follow feature edges only.
- **Points:** only **feature points** are pickable: corners where feature edges meet, the end points of open feature-edge chains, and (where a mode asks for it) arc/circle centres derived from a round feature edge. Interior mesh vertices are never pickable.
- **Visible first, never through:** a pick resolves to the front-most visible surface under the cursor (the same depth the viewport draws, perspective and ortho). An edge or point is pickable only if it is visible there (not occluded by the model, within a small screen-space tolerance of the front surface). Nothing on the far side is picked unless the user explicitly turns on a "pick through" mode, which is off by default and shown as such.
- **Snapping order near a feature:** within the pick radius, prefer point, then edge, then face, but **only** among the kinds the current tool accepts (e.g. plane alignment is faces only after #554; axis by edge or two points takes edges/points). A tool that doesn't accept edges never snaps to one.
- **One implementation:** a single picking service in the app layer (feature graph: welded faces, feature edges, feature points; visibility test against the depth the viewport uses) that every UI picker (`plane_pick`, `edge_pick`, `vertex_pick`, `axis_pick`, fixture locate, origin/WCS picks) and the MCP pick tools call. No page carries its own picking rules.

## Done means
- A shared feature-graph and pick API in the app layer, with tests:
  - a flat face's triangulation edges are not pickable;
  - a cylinder's facet edges are not pickable but its circular rim is;
  - a box corner is a pickable point, while a vertex inside a face isn't;
  - a feature edge on the far side of the part is not picked through the near face, in both perspective and ortho;
  - "pick through", when explicitly on, does pick it.
- Every UI picker and the MCP pick tools use it (no local pick logic left); UI tests on the setup page, op geometry and fixture locate confirm the behaviour.
- A short note in the user docs (#688) on what a click picks.

Related: #554 (plane picks faces only), #557 (axis by edge/points), #555 (three points), #561/#566 (fixture locate), #180 (MCP picks), #241 (selecting on complex planar faces), #613/#609/#610 (ortho rays).

title: Post gate refuses a Bore at a STEP hole's own size: the sim charges the 0.02 mm facet sagitta as a 20 mm gouge

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
A Bore on a modelled hole, at the hole's own size, is refused by the post gate as a **20 mm gouge**. The operation's own verify finds nothing. The overcut being charged is the gap between the true circle the bore cuts and the inscribed facets of the imported mesh, about 0.02 mm sideways.

**Reproduction** (main b57f8d52, Windows, `camcraft-cli mcp`):

```
import_model   {"path":"testdata/models/Milling-test.step","name":"part"}
set_stock      {"from_model":"part"}
add_tool       {"catalog":"EM-1000-4FL"}
add_operation  {"kind":"bore","tool":"EM-1000-4FL","source":"part","name":"OP"}
detect_holes   {"name":"OP"}        -> 1 hole: xy (0, 0), radius 12.5, entry z 20, floor z 0
generate       {"name":"OP"}        -> status ok, 0 warnings
verify         {}
```

`verify` returns no per-op finding. The program gate says:

```
gouge: program cuts below the model in 1 cell(s), worst 20.00 mm at (4.69, 11.59, z 0.00)
```

(4.69, 11.59) is at r = 12.50, on the hole wall. The same happens with EM-0800-4FL (1 cell, 20.00 mm at (11.76, -4.23)) and EM-0600-4FL (4 cells, 20.00 mm at (9.57, -8.04)).

**Neighbour cases that still work:**
- The same bore with `"stock_to_leave": 0.01` verifies clean, and so do 0.015, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5. With 0.005 it is still refused.
- A 2D Contour around the part's outside (convex walls) on the same finished-part setup passes the gate.

**Root cause (likely):** the STEP mesh is coarser than the gouge verdict.
- `list_features` on the part shows the Ø25 hole wall as 53 flat strips, 6.79° each. The chord sagitta is 12.5 × (1 − cos 3.40°) = **0.022 mm**.
- The STEP importer meshes to a chord tolerance of `extent * 1e-3` (`crates/app/src/geometry/import/step.rs`, `tol_target`), about 0.06 mm for this 60 mm part.
- The program sim judges against those facets with `tol` = `GOUGE_TOL` = 0.01 mm (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/deviate.rs`, `deviate`). The sideways slack from #299 (`wall_slack.rs`) is the same 0.01 mm.
- On a concave curved wall the facets lie inside the true surface. A bore that cuts the true r = 12.5 therefore removes up to 0.022 mm of "model" between chord and arc. That is past the 0.01 slack, so the column is charged the wall's full 20 mm height.

The sagitta (0.022) against the threshold (stock_to_leave 0.01 plus tol 0.01) matches where the refusal stops. That is why this says "likely" and not "confirmed".

Any finishing pass that meets a concave curved wall at nominal size should hit the same thing: bores, a contour inside a round boss pocket, round internal corners. A larger part has a coarser mesh (extent/1000), so its sagitta is larger.

Done means: a bore at a STEP hole's nominal size verifies clean, a bore 0.05 mm oversize into the same wall is still refused, and both are pinned by tests.

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

body:
## What happens
When CamCraft is started from a terminal, the terminal tells you almost nothing
about what the app is doing. There is no logging framework in the workspace at
all: no `log` or `tracing` dependency in any Cargo.toml, no subscriber
init in the binaries - just ~185 ad-hoc `println!`/`eprintln!` calls scattered
across crates (cli.rs, gpu_init.rs, shell.rs, the post bin). If a subsystem
decides, refuses, retries, or fails to write a file, no line reaches the
console and the failure is only discovered later by forensics on the output.

## Why now (session of 2026-11-07)
Two incidents this week were diagnosed only by reading source afterwards,
because the console was silent during them:
- **A file did not get saved when post processing** - the post appeared to
  succeed; nothing in the terminal said which path it wrote (or that it wrote
  nothing at all).
- **A limit was hit while generating operations** - the generator aborted on a
  budget/limit; the terminal showed no trace of which cap fired or what the
  result was downgraded to.

Prime Directive says "log diagnostics, never silence" - today we cannot.

## Expected
The launching terminal streams debug-level logs of app activity, filterable:
- project save / post write: source path, destination, bytes, or the reason
  nothing was written;
- operation generation: start, end, duration, which limits/budgets stopped a
  generator and what fallback took over;
- verify/sim refusals: the rule that fired and the numbers behind it;
- commands executing (name + affected entities) at debug level.

## Suggested shape
`tracing` + `tracing_subscriber` fmt layer writing to stderr at startup of the
UI binary, default level `info`, overridable by `RUST_LOG` (or a camcraft
config/env of our own). Instrument the command dispatch seam, generators, and
post entry points - the crates are already split (M4.1), so each takes its own
span targets (`camcraft_app::post`, `camcraft_motion::adaptive`, ...). Keep
hot generation loops behind level gates - logging must not slow generation.

## Done means
- Launching the app and running a post writes terminal lines naming the file
  path and result; a failed/skipped write says why.
- Hitting a generation budget (e.g. an Adaptive limit) prints which limit and
  what happened next.
- Levels are controlled by env var, default output stays quiet at `info`, and
  the batch gate shows no measurable generation slowdown.

Found while debugging the post-save incident (user request, 2026-11-07).

title: 2D Adaptive trochoid: land microlift returns on air, and a practical step for thin bands

labels.name: blocked

body:
Follow-up from #5 round 2 (staged on worktree agent-af493aee8d4f2d538, gated off).

The trochoid fallback (spiral -> trochoid -> rings) is wired in `pocket_hsm` / `pocket_troch` and plans the 22x60 channel end to end. One law keeps it off:

1. **Landing law (one descent per level).** Each microlift return ramps down onto the next front arc's start. That start is already in cut: the crescent ahead and the 0.33 mm wall strip are both inside the measuring rim (r + 1.5 cells). So `quality` counts a descent into stock every loop (118 for 2 levels against the law's 2). The spiral's lifted pieces avoid this with air leads. Trochoid arcs have no air lead that crosses no floor feed: a floor lead from inside the cleared area to the next start crosses the previous arc. Options to try: arcs whose ends sweep the wall strip clean (rho * sin(h) = half-width) plus a start ramp along the arc's own circle extension (crossing-free up to 90 deg + asin(s / 2 rho)), or non-circular loops whose start lies behind the previous envelope. Pinned by `troch_tests::a_landing_on_a_loop_start_in_cut_is_refused_by_name`. Remove the law's refusal once it holds.
2. **A practical step for thin bands (#13's 14 mm band).** It reads rho 1.90, s 0.103 and 2575 loops a level at the load. That is over the `LOOP_CAP` (600) and, before that, has no room to open out behind a helix. A closed band's trochoid is also not wired yet. It stays on the named Offset-rings fallback.
3. The 3-D ladder (`machining3d::hsm`) does not try the trochoid yet (`adaptive_passes(.., false)`).
